points.text: A testable statement predicting the outcome of a statistical investigation.

questions.question: Q: What does the null hypothesis state?

points.text: That there is no difference, no effect or no relationship between the variables being studied.

questions.question: Q: Write a suitable hypothesis for investigating whether Year 11 students spend more time on homework than Year 10 students.

points.text: Year 11 students spend more time on homework per week than Year 10 students.

questions.question: Q: Why must a hypothesis be testable?

points.text: So that data can be collected and analysed to determine whether the prediction is supported or not.

questions.question: Q: What is the difference between an independent and a dependent variable?

points.text: The independent variable is the one you change or categorise; the dependent variable is the one you measure or observe.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response A student wants to investigate whether people who exercise regularly have a lower resting heart rate. Write a suitable hypothesis and identify the variables. <div class="

points.text: Hypothesis: People who exercise regularly have a lower resting heart rate than those who do not exercise regularly. Independent variable: Whether the person exercises regularly (categorised as 'exercises regularly' or 'does not exercise regularly'). Dependent variable: Resting heart rate (measured in beats per minute). The hypothesis is testable because both variables can be measured: exercise habits can be categorised and resting heart rate can be recorded. Data from both groups can then be compared using an appropriate diagram and summary statistic.
